First of all the spectator system and character designs force unwanted content on players. The moment you die the camera automatically forces you to spectate teammates. Second is the major technical flaw in the disconnection and penalty system. If your internet stutters for just a single second the game immediately kicks you out completely. Reconnecting takes so much time that you end up getting slapped with an unfair match ban.

Why is the system so unforgiving? In other games like CSGO a brief internet drop does not throw you out of the game entirely. You stay in the match and resume playing immediately once the connection stabilizes within seconds. Why is there such a massive punishing difference in Overwatch 2?

These issues need immediate attention and developers must add proper settings and toggles that respect players time and preferences.

Overwatch is still one of the smoothest and most enjoyable competitive games I’ve played.

The optimization is excellent. The game runs incredibly smoothly even on lower-end hardware, while still looking great. The gameplay is fast-paced, matches usually don’t take too long, and there’s very little downtime, so it’s very easy to jump in for a few games without committing an entire evening.

Competitive mode is intense and genuinely competitive. The ranking system does a pretty good job of creating close and challenging matches, and climbing the ranks can be extremely satisfying.

Quick Play is surprisingly fun as well. A lot of players still take it seriously, so it sometimes feels like Competitive mode for people who just want to escape Competitive for a while.

The character skins are also excellent. Blizzard does a great job keeping the designs consistent with each hero’s personality and overall theme instead of simply throwing random cosmetics into the game.

Gameplay mechanics are generally well balanced considering how many heroes, abilities, counters, maps, and team compositions exist. Obviously, perfect balance is impossible in a game like this, but overall it feels surprisingly well managed.

Blizzard’s punishment system is also pretty strict when it comes to players who break the rules, leave games, or behave badly. Personally, I think that helps keep the experience healthier.

The community is actually pretty good too, especially compared with many other competitive online games. Of course there are toxic players occasionally, but overall my experience with the player base has been very positive.

And somehow, after all this time, I still haven’t encountered an obvious hacker. That alone deserves some credit.

Another big reason the game stays fresh is the constant introduction of new heroes. New characters, abilities, and team compositions keep changing how the game plays, so it rarely feels boring. This year in particular has been great in that regard.

Although Blizzard... maybe give Support players a little more love next time? Haha.

There are still a few things I don’t like.

The biggest problem is that there are simply too many game modes. Arcade especially feels overcrowded with different modes, which spreads the player base too thin instead of concentrating players into a few strong playlists.

The other issue is that the game still seems unable to fully decide whether it wants to be 5v5 or 6v6. Supporting both formats sounds good in theory, but in practice it divides the matchmaking population even further. When the player base is already smaller than it used to be, splitting players between two major formats can make matchmaking feel unnecessarily fragmented.

Overall, though, Overwatch remains incredibly fun, polished, competitive, and easy to keep coming back to. Very few games manage to combine fast gameplay, strong hero design, good optimization, competitive depth, and this much variety as well as Overwatch does.

Really good game at its base, but developers try their best to make it worse at every turn.

The good:
1. Perfect sound design and soundmaster.
Never ever have I found a PvP game that gets this as good as OW; I get about 50% of my info through sound. Especially compared to Marvel rivals, it's night and day

2. Beautiful character and map design.
The characters have unique visuals and stories, the same with the maps. It does this while keeping competitive integrity. 

3. Hero designs are fun but are still mostly fair to play against.

The bad:

1. 5v5: As an OG, 5v5 is a clear downgrade in team play, and while you have the option to play 6v6, it gets held back by all the global systems still in place for the 5v5 mode.

2. Monetization: Horrendously overpriced skins and a price structure that does not make sense at all: A 10€ Battle Pass gets you like 8 skins and a mythic skin (80€ on its own). At the same time, they want to sell you worse mythics or ultra skins for 40€. Luckily, if you don't care about skins, all the other actual content is free. The saving grace here is the free loot boxes that can give you skins from last year for free.

3. Ranked: Ranked is actually really good at making balanced matches and putting you in the right elo. But there is no reward for actually being good. All the reward is just for playtime. Even the top 500 leaderboard is just the list of players that play the most, not the ones that are the highest ranked.

Comparison to Marvel rivals:
If you are looking for a competitive game, Overwatch is the clear winner; the ranked mode is far more balanced and closer to a balanced Elo system, is way more readable and has better net code.  For a more casual game, OW is more readable, but Rivals offers more content in the same timeframe, so you can pick what you like more. If you like more story in games, I think Rivals is way better since they have all the comics.
In terms of monetization, I think it's about the same since rivals force you to gamble for some skins, which is always going to be scummy. Overwatch also runs about twice as well on my overkill PC and runs a lot better on older machines.

Overall, I recommend Overwatch. Even if it gets held back by most of the stuff they introduced in OW2. But just because it's worse than the original game does not mean it's bad, its still good. Don't let the mixed reviews fool you, it's mostly people rightfully wishing back the old times.

No, I'm not talking about Overwatch 2--I'm talking about the legendary [i]Heroes of the Storm[/i].
The community for that game has persisted through so much, the iconic 6.5/10 IGN review, constant shade from the more established MOBA fanbases, and nearly 6 years of only getting minor bugfixes and small balance patches. When Blizzard announced Esports were cancelled and that HotS was going into maintainance mode just as it seemed the game was really popping off, I was gutted. Thousands of hours of awesome collaboration and competition with my friends, and Blizzard seemed to just abandon the game. How often do you see someone with thousands of hours in a MOBA singing its praises? It's mostly just doomposting from those communities. Anyways, I continued to play the game every once in a while, and it was always a good time, but it doesn't mean it didn't hurt to see Blizzard's gigantic franchises like WoW and Overwatch get all the attention, when HotS, despite its success, just didn't seem to be big enough for Blizzard.

Even before maintainance mode, I always sort of had the feeling that a lot of the heart and soul of Blizzard had been dwindling, but HotS was the sparkle of hope in my mind--the updates always felt so full of passion and love for the rich history and iconic experiences that Blizzard is known for. When they seemingly abandoned the game, I thought all hope was lost. The company I once knew and loved was gone, replaced with a soulless husk that delivers nothing but more mediocre-at-best expansions for WoW, the mostly maligned-by-the-community Overwatch 2, and scandals about the frat-bro SA culture at the company. I put Blizzard behind me, thinking all was lost. 

But come Blizzcon 2026, I could tell something was different. I don't know what it was, but I decided to tune in for the first time in many, many years. I didn't have high hopes for Heroes of the Storm content, but I guess I just decided to watch anyways, at the very least for the other announcements. And boy I'm glad I did. Blizzard, for some unknown reason, decided to START THE SHOW WITH A NEW HERO ANNOUNCEMENT FOR HOTS. Somehow, despite the odds, the man the community dubbed "The Janitor" had managed to assemble a team to bring some real honest-to-god new content to the game after all this time. James Yen, as he turned out to be, seems pretty optimistic about HotS being sustainable in the future too, so we'll probably be getting more content in the near future.

On top of some other exciting announcements for WoW, Diablo, and Starcraft, this new announcement rekindled my hope for the company--if Blizzard saw value in reviving this "dead game", then anything was possible. I'm cautiously optimistic for the time being, but it feels like Blizzard is finally back on a good track again after having their reputation dragged through the mud. The result of all this is that I ended up purchasing a few things from Blizzard, something I haven't done in years, and I also downloaded and tried Overwatch, having not played since around when Doomfist was released. Honestly--this game is in a wayyyyy better state than it used to be in. The skins are way overpriced, but whatever. The game is fun. I've been having a good time so far.

If you're a fan of Overwatch, but feeling like you've played too much of this game, or just wanna branch out, I encourage you to get the Battle.net launcher and play some Heroes of the Storm. MOBAs can be a pretty intimidating genre, but Heroes of the Storm is by far the best for newcomers--no item shop, short-and-sweet 20-minute matches, and a hero pool which is much easier to familiarize yourself with due to most of them being characters from existing Blizzard properties. It's a great time, and lots of new players are starting now due to the hype, so there hasn't been a better time to start your journey in a long while. 

I hope you have fun, and I'll see you in the Nexus :)

Overwatch delivers an incredibly engaging and fast-paced hero-shooter experience that keeps you coming back for more. With a rich roster of unique heroes, dynamic team synergies, and vibrant map designs, every match feels fresh, competitive, and highly entertaining. Whether you are coordinating ultimate abilities or clutching a last-second objective contest, the core gameplay loop is exceptionally satisfying.

What Makes It Great

High Replayability & Teamwork: The game truly shines when playing with friends. Strategizing hero compositions, pulling off combo plays, and communicating on the fly make it an ideal game to drop into anytime for a quick session or a weekend gaming marathon.

Diverse Playstyles: Each hero offers a distinct set of abilities, allowing players to find a role—whether Tank, Damage, or Support—that perfectly suits their preferred style of play.

Room for Improvement

Matchmaking Balance: While the core mechanics are solid, the matchmaking system could definitely use some fine-tuning. You occasionally run into unbalanced matches where the skill gap between teams feels a bit too steep, leading to one-sided games.

Technical Glitches: There is also a minor bug where login errors occasionally pop up, temporarily blocking access to the game. While it doesn't happen every time, it can be a bit frustrating when you are trying to jump straight into action.

Overall, despite a few technical hiccups and matchmaking quirks, Overwatch remains a fantastic, highly addictive game that offers endless entertainment—especially when played alongside friends. Highly recommended for anyone looking for a polished team-based shooter.

I have 1900+ hours on this game at time of writing (played on Battlenet before the steam version released). Overwatch is a game that has something for everyone, of any skill level. If you are bad at aiming in FPS games, there are characters where you do not need to aim. If you on the other hand like fast paced combat, enjoy aiming and going bang bang with your weapon, there is a lot of variety also in which ways you wish to do that. There is a very large cast of characters, all of them do very different things (mostly) each character has unique abilities, voice lines, animations, cosmetics, perks, etc. There are a vast amount of different game modes in the arcade if you don't like the regular quick play, or competitive modes. Or you can use the game browser to find custom games, or make one yourself. There is also a practice/firing range for you to try out every character in the game, and see what they do before you play against real people. You can also set up a practice match vs bots if that still isn't enough for you. There is an in game match/team chat, both voice and text. I recommend ignoring these completely if you are new to the game, as people get very angry over silly things that make no sense (we're on the internet after all). I've described each character in Overwatch before like playing a different game, because of how differently they all feel to play, so you'll never run out of variety. Each character has a specific role: Tank, Damage (often called DPS), and Support. In quick play or standard ranked, both teams have 1 Tank, 2 Damage, and 2 Support players. This is a a good thing. I started playing the game when the role queue system did not exist. You would queue into a game and no one would want to play as a healer, so your team would just die if you didn't choose to suck it up and play Support to heal them and keep them alive. Role queue has eliminated this problem entirely. If you want to see what it felt like without this, there is an open queue mode, where there are no restrictions on roles. I only advise playing this if you are prepared to endure what I have just spoken about. Overall, I think Overwatch is a great game. You can play it with friends, make new ones, or play alone. There is something for everyone as I have said, and even if you're not "good" at FPS video games, this does not matter, as you can find a character that you like, and suits how you play, and become good at them and learn them. And also, this is a video game. It's really not important at all if you're good or bad. A game is something that is meant to be played for fun. Don't forget that. And please do not ever let anyone ruin your fun, in any video game. If you do play the competitive mode, you are expected to play to your best, so do try in this mode, or people will report you. It's good to have a few characters that you are comfortable playing before doing competitive, so that if someone takes your character, you have someone else that you can play. Anyway, give the game a go since it's free. I'm sure there will be something that you enjoy about it.

Overwatch 2 is a game that had a huge amount of potential, but in my opinion, that potential has been completely wasted. While the actual gameplay mechanics can be fun and the characters are interesting, almost everything surrounding the game leaves a very bad impression. One of the biggest problems is the matchmaking. Far too often, one team feels like they know exactly what they are doing, while the other team has absolutely no coordination. Because of this, matches can feel extremely unfair and frustrating. Instead of feeling like a victory is the result of my own skill and effort, it often feels like the outcome depends on luck.

Another huge problem is the price of skins and other cosmetic items. The prices are simply ridiculous for what you actually get. Some skins cost an absurd amount of money, especially when compared to other games. The game may be free-to-play, but it often feels like almost everything is designed to encourage players to spend money.

The Battle Pass is not particularly impressive either. Instead of making players feel rewarded for playing the game, it often feels like another way to monetize the player base. On top of that, the hero balancing can be terrible at times. Some characters can be ridiculously overpowered, while others feel almost completely useless, which makes matches even more frustrating.

There are also plenty of annoying issues such as toxic players, smurfs, leavers, and teammates who give up as soon as the match starts going badly. All of this can turn an otherwise normal game into a miserable experience.

Overall, Overwatch 2 feels like a game that is more focused on making money than providing players with a fair and enjoyable experience. The gameplay can be fun, but the terrible matchmaking, overpriced skins, Battle Pass, balancing issues, and general frustration ruin the experience. If you have a lot of patience and really love hero shooters, you might still enjoy it, but personally, I would recommend playing something else.

I will start off by saying that this is probably (unfortunately) my most played game, and for the most part it is very fun. That being said, this game has numerous issues as well as horrible cosmetic pricing.

1. To start, the cosmetic pricing is egregious, with the best skins (mythic) costing $80 to buy outright. Any game developer who thinks that a single character skin is worth more than a modern triple-A game is full of themselves. Buying a normal skin generally costs around $20, which is still terrible. The only thing that is well-priced is the battle pass, which comes with enough mythic coins to get a mythic skin. Following that metric, mythic skins should cost at most $10, and the legendary skins should be $2-5 at most. Also, as a tip for the devs: If y’all lower prices to a reasonable level, sales quantity and player satisfaction would jump significantly. The increased sales volume would probably offset the price decrease to allow for higher revenue as well.

2. Moving to the next issue and adding fuel to the flame, many of the expensive mythic skins are not very good. They are supposedly customizable skins, but 90% of the time that just means that you can change the hair, and that it has the option to have some random energy glow that feels more and more tacky and ugly with each new skin. I also don’t love that they are doing repeat characters for the mythic skins, but I understand that they will always prioritize more popular or iconic characters.

3. The final major issue lies with the matchmaking. For one, this game is completely incapable of matchmaking when you have friends with significantly differing skill levels. The game will give you opponents that are far beyond what your team can go against, and you will not enjoy the game at all. If someone in your group is at a higher skill level, then the only real option is for them to play on an alt account. I have other issues with the matchmaking as well, but I understand that most of the matchmaking mechanics are designed to get you to keep playing regardless of how fair or fun the matches are.

Overall, I wish I could give this game a good review. Many of the characters are very fun, the events are great, and the OW team does their best to keep characters balanced (even if their balancing decisions sometimes make no sense). I will unfortunately continue to play this game simply because many of my friends play it.

[h1]A love-hate relationship.[/h1]

Is probably the best way to describe Overwatch. I'm not even sure where to [i]begin[/i] with the game, it has a fair bit of good, but it also has a [b]lot[/b] of bad as well.

So I'll focus on a few things:
[list]
[*] Problematic Heroes
[*] Balancing
[*] Matchmaking
[/list]

[h2]Problematic Heroes.[/h2]

The heroes in this game are naturally diverse and varied, but in recent months they've released a hero that breaks [b]all[/b] the rules of the game:

[i]Jetpack Cat.[/i]

Now as you can surmise its a cat in a jetpack, but what makes it so awful and bad is that it breaks the fundamental rule that Overwatch had since day 1: [b]No. Permanent. Flying.[/b] every hero that has the ability to fly is tied to a timer or a resource bar of some kind, but Jetpack Cat seemingly ignores this rule and can fly infinitely [b]and[/b] have a boost mode as well. This by itself is already quite a jarring experience, maps aren't built for perma-flying and it shows:
[list]
[*] The skybox is pretty low, barely allowing them to fly over maps
[*] Jetpack Cat can hide behind buildings indefinitely at a high elevation that you can't reach even with other flying characters, let alone grounded ones
[*] Jetpack cat can quite literally hide under sections of the map that are inaccessible unless you want to die trying (and failing) to kill them with any hero outside of another Jetpack Cat
[/list]

To put it simply: Jetpack Cat is probably the most frustrating hero to fight against in the game as it stands (excluding skilled players on specific heroes). If that wasn't bad enough, Jetpack Cat is a [b]support[/b] hero, so they have the ability to heal themselves as well as their team, but their whole kit enables and encourages her to be the perfect flanker that can't be easily dealt with, with a 225 health pool to boot, a small hitbox, and long range weapons, you'll be struggling with this feline. Her support function is being able to [b]carry teammates[/b] into the air [b]indefinitely[/b], allowing some heroes that were clearly never intended to have high speed to just be zipped around the map because of a tiny cat.

To rub salt in the wound, someone at Blizzard is clearly aware of how annoying this cat would be and went the extra mile to add a [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ejbeOEbRaLQ]"taunting" voice line[/url] for players to use, just to add some psychological warfare to the game.

[h3]Is that the only hero?[/h3]

No. There's definitely other problematic heroes but this would be rather long, but as a quick rapid-fire:
[list]
[*] Freja: Damage class that can leap up and pretty much instant-kill you in 0.7 seconds with several explosive arrows that stick to you
[*] Mauga: Tank class that has 2 chainguns, can stomp on you, and heal from shooting you
[*] Zarya: Tank class that can put a bubble around teammates that acts as a shield and also makes her weapon stronger, effectively fueling your own demise and killing you quickly
[*] Roadhog: Tank class that can self-heal back to full on the move, has a hook to bring you into his lethal range (1-shot shotgun), and even at range he has a secondary fire that can snipe you at medium distances.
[/list]

These are heroes that are considered to have a lot of pain points in the community and are seen as problematic (If you play competitive modes, you'll frequently see these banned, especially Jetpack Cat whom had a 70% global ban rate even at the top competitive levels), it makes you wonder that surely Blizzard would do something... Well...

[h2]Balancing[/h2]

...Now with the above heroes mentioned, the logical next step is to think

[quote]"Surely Blizzard would make adjustments so these heroes aren't annoying to play against?"[/quote]

And you'd be right! Except there's one problem:

Blizzard seems to be concerned about balancing at the [b]esports level, [u]not[/u] at the casual level.[/b] What I mean by that is you won't really see nerfs or buffs to heroes unless they're being used in esports competitive play (Like the Overwatch World Championships) where top players will have grinded these heroes to a fine art and have tech levels that you can't grasp, I've seen some of these games and the gameplay is [b]so. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ fast.[/b] that if you blink you genuinely might miss some stuff.

The problem with this naturally is the heroes that should be addressed... Don't, and the ones that are perfectly fine for the casual crowd... [i]Get adjusted.[/i] In the latest update (September 8 2026) they have made inconsequential nerfs to a couple of the heroes mentioned earlier, but then they have decided to nerf or buff other heroes that had no issues at all. Some of these changes were 'fine' as they wouldn't make a difference, but others you can clearly tell they were done in response to esports play and not how the playerbase plays them (e.g teleporter distances being reduced, cooldowns for certain heroes being increased, making a [i]literal sound adjustment?)[/i]

This is despite many complaints from the playerbase about many heroes, which you can find either here on the [steam discussions or better yet on the Overwatch Forums ( https://us.forums.blizzard.com/en/overwatch/c/general-discussion/6 )

[h2]Matchmaking[/h2]

This is just short, sweet, and simple:

The matchmaking sucks.

There's nothing to sugarcoat, you might be fine initially playing but you'll find yourself quickly playing a lot of games where all you see is this:

[b]DEFEAT[/b]

Why? Well for some reason the matchmaking loves to decide to pit you against [b]very experienced[/b] players. I've had games where I am fighting with or against [b]Top 500 competitive players[/b] in Overwatch, quite literally the best, of the best, and Blizzard thinks I can go up against them [spoiler]I can't. They wreck me or make me look pathetic.[/spoiler] it makes games feel like a genuine gamble and the worst part is you can tell within the first 30 - 60 seconds of a game if you even have a [b]slither[/b] of a chance of playing, let alone winning the game.

It has gotten to the point where people have said the following:
[list]
[*] "Quickplay is the real competitive mode"
[*] "Play competitive if you want balanced matchmaking"
[/list]

This has lead into a LOT of theories that the game attempts to keep your general win/loss ratio at a neat 50%, if you try going above that you [b]BETTER[/b] be John Overwatch and carry your team otherwise you'll be humbled pretty fast, if you try to lose games you don't have to worry because even if you do nothing you might still win on account of having that carry on your team. Put simply: The matchmaking does not feel balanced at all, it is a genuine coin toss, you can tell pretty quickly how games go, and in the 'casual' mode you'll be playing against people that are playing as if $1,000,000 are on the line [b]every. game.[/b]

[h2]So why do you play?[/h2]

Because I do find some fun with it, despite how toxic some people can be (You WILL be finding toxic people, trust me), I do have some small, nice conversations, and Overwatch has a nice feel with its movement that I just haven't really felt in a good while. Plus when you get that natural co-ordination with people you've never met, it genuinely feels great when you get that synchronisation.

I've had some funny moments and [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3766737867]witnessed[/url] some [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3798363609]funny moments[/url] too that were [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3782007315]screenshot worthy[/url] that you just can't replicate or force, they just happen in the wild.

But, it is like I said, a love-hate relationship. There's a few goods, but honestly... There's a lot of bad. [b]If you plan to get into this, you should expect to be constantly saying "FFS!" a lot.[/b] Its a game that shouldn't be taken seriously, yet somehow I keep finding myself doing so.

Overwatch is well and truly a 50/50 game. There are many things that make the game worth coming back to, but just as many things that make you want to kill yourself. 

+ The game is very well optimised in comparison to other esports titlet (MR comes to mind). With a modest, maybe even an outdated, dedicated gpu and somewhat modern cpu you can get well over 60 fps even in chaotic teamfights.
+ Many maps that have different nuances and allow for a wide variety of team compositions, there are no decided metas for every role (except for kiri)
+ Learning the characters details, strenghts and weaknesses allow for plays that feel just as rewarding every time you do them. 
+ The developers seem to somewhat care about the game. Their heart is in the right place but their minds are on Neptune

- Matchmaking is horrendous. The ranked system is probably, tied with some outstanding character balancing issues, the biggest problem this game has at the moment. This season is probably the worst season yet matchmaking wise. I went from Diamond 1 to Diamond 5 in about two weeks time. 
- Some characters are in desperate need of reworks/balancing. Kiri, Mauga and Hazard are some that come to mind. Kiri has been meta since she came out four years ago. 
- The amount of the attention that some characters receive cosmetics-wise is honestly disturbing. Kiriko, Mercy and Juno have received about one billion skins each while Wrecking Balls most recent legendary skin was 800 days ago.
- The community is a mixed bag. Either kind normal people (one in a krillion), femboy support players or absolute cretinous homonculi that mimic human sounds and actions. No inbetween.

All in all it is a good game that has some really engaging gameplay.

I used to play Overwatch back when it first came out in 2016. Before then, I didn't really care for multiplayer games. Overwatch changed that and became the most fun I ever had with an online game. Then the Blitzchung incident happen, and that was the breaking point for me. Not only had the game become miserable for casuals, but now the company itself was horribly crooked and immoral. And that ended up being the least controversial thing that was discovered about Blizzard at the time.

10 years later, Blizzard itself had changed, and Overwatch had finally found the sauce agian. Bringing back 6v6, adding new features because they're fun and not because it would be 'competetivly viable like Stadium and Jetpack Cat, ACTUALLY WRITING A REAL STORY WITH ACTUAL PROGRESSION!

The newest season and the addition of another mech-pilot waifu was finally the breaking point for me to redownload this game. As long as you can link your old battlenet account to steam, ALL of your progress and possessions transfer over. I was honestly prepared to start from scratch but returning feels like coming back to your old hometown. Some things have changed, there's plenty of new faces, but it still feels like home.

My 2nd ever match I encountered a team that had Jetpack Cat tethering a Pharah allowing her to stay in the air indefinatly camping the payload. My immediate thought was- "This is so stupid... This game is SO BACK!"

It took 10 years of growing pains, but Overwatch finally remembered what makes itself so fun and embraces it.
